https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher, who closed the SDS when he was at Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA View image in fullscreen PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher, who closed the SDS when he was at Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA Spycops scandal Undercover police and policing Undercover police unit closed down over unjustified surveillance, spycops inquiry told Senior officer behind closure says SDS caused ‘incalculable harm’ by infiltrating groups that posed no threat Rob Evans Sun 2 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 01.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An undercover police unit that spied on tens of thousands of political activists had to be shut down amid severe criticisms and recriminations, the spycops public inquiry has heard. Jon Boutcher, a senior police officer who took over responsibility for the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS) unit, concluded within months that it had to be wound up because it was conducting unjustified surveillance and was badly run. He said most of the political groups being infiltrated “posed no threat to public order, let alone democracy”. They included pro-Palestinian supporters and leftwing groups. In contrast, very few undercover officers were being directed to infiltrate terrorist groups, he said. “At that time, society faced an increasing and enduring threat from international terrorism from which people were losing their lives, while almost no undercover capability existed to infiltrate those dangerous terrorist groups.” Boutcher, who was a detective chief superintendent in Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorist division at the time and is now the chief constable of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, said the unit had to be closed down “pretty quickly”. Undercover police officer exposed by his own blunder, spycops inquiry hears Read more The SDS had once been lauded as a “jewel in the crown” of Scotland Yard by its supporters within senior ranks. In searing criticism from an officer who has been involved in leading covert policing for years, Boutcher said the “abusive and inappropriate behaviour” of the SDS undercover officers had damaged members of the public. The officers routinely formed intimate relationships with women they were spying on without telling them their real identities. Boutcher said the “sexual abuse of many vulnerable women by some SDS operatives” caused “incalculable and intolerable harm”. He said the SDS should never have spied on grieving families, such as the relatives of Jean Charles de Menezes, the innocent man shot dead by police on the London Underground in 2005. Nor should they have collected highly intrusive information about protesters, such as their friendships and living arrangements. View image in fullscreen A memorial to Jean Charles de Menezes outside Stockwell tube station in London. Boutcher said the SDS should never have spied on the dead man’s family. Photograph: Stephen Kelly/PA The inquiry is examining the conduct of 139 undercover officers in the SDS and another covert unit who infiltrated mainly leftwing organisations between 1968 and at least 2010. They assumed fake identities and pretended to be political activists in deployments that usually lasted four years. This week the inquiry heard how, in its final days, there was a “toxic” atmosphere between the unit and the more senior Scotland Yard ranks. Boutcher, with the agreement of his superiors, disbanded the SDS in what he called “quite a groundbreaking” decision as it had been running covert operations for 40 years. He said the SDS mounted “almost like a rearguard action” to justify its existence in what he characterised as a “very much siege mentality in many ways”. He said he suspected the SDS was gathering an “extremely limited” amount of useful information, and asked the unit to draw up a list of its successes in the previous five years. During that time, the undercover officers had spied on environment groups, the Socialist Workers party and campaigns against racism and the arms trade. The purported triumphs that were put forward by the SDS were “embellished and exaggerated”, almost “akin to fairytales”, Boutcher said. He also said he was concerned that public money allocated to the unit was not properly accounted for. The officers were claiming “vast amounts of overtime”, he said. When drastic cuts to these payments were proposed, many of them threatened to resign, the inquiry heard. Boutcher said the unit was poorly trained, and all but one of the undercover officers refused to undergo further training. Initially, Boutcher believed the SDS could be reformed and in particular re-oriented to infiltrate terrorist groups. But he concluded this was not possible because the SDS had become “insular and very parochial” and was resistant to change. https://www.politico.eu/article/post-orb.text: BRUSSELS — EU ambassadors will make another push Wednesday to finalize the bloc’s first Russia sanctions package since Viktor Orbán left office, after governments stripped back key measures to protect their energy, fish processing, banking and shipping interests. For years, Orbán — Hungary’s veteran populist leader who cultivated close ties with the Kremlin and repeatedly threatened to block sanctions — gave other capitals cover to resist tougher action. With Péter Magyar now leading Hungary and Budapest no longer standing in the way, those governments are being forced to defend their objections in the open. “It has been a surprise and a disappointment how many member states have stalled in their actions,” said Ville Niinistö, a Finnish MEP and chair of the European Parliament’s Russia delegation. “It is of utmost importance to continue strengthening the EU sanctions against Russia in this moment when Russia is starting to feel the pressure of the war in its domestic economy and in public perception.” Advertisement Advertisement A deal is still broadly expected, but more concessions may be needed before ambassadors can get it over the line. Seven people working on the package told POLITICO that several measures had already been weakened or dropped altogether. The package, presented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in June, is the 21st since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. After 20 previous rounds, diplomats say the EU is running out of easy targets and increasingly colliding with powerful national interests. Sanctions require the unanimous backing of all 27 EU countries. “There’s no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done. You’ll bump into individual member state interests more, so you have to find a balance,” said an EU diplomat involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to discuss the confidential talks, like others in this article. Greece has so far refused to support the 21st package because of a ban on EU companies shipping Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries. Athens oversees the world’s largest merchant fleet and is concerned about the impact on a Greek company that operates ice-breaking tankers that export Russian LNG. Greece’s ambassador warned that the measure could prompt vessels to reflag and move to jurisdictions where the rules would be even harder to enforce, according to two further diplomats involved in the discussions. “We’re trying to find a way out of this, but what this [issue with Greece] shows is that we’re starting to collide with some key economic interests,” said a fourth diplomat. Advertisement Advertisement Along with Malta and Cyprus, Greece had also hesitated over a six-month extension of the freeze on the $44.10-per-barrel price cap on Russian oil. EU countries bought themselves more time by keeping the cap frozen until Thursday, and the extension is now expected to pass if a solution is found for the Greek veto on LNG shipments. Troubled waters The talks were also roiled by an Austrian intervention on behalf of Raiffeisen Bank, the second largest in the country. Raiffeisen has long sought compensation for what it calls the illegal €2.44 billion expropriation of its assets in Russia through the transfer of frozen funds belonging to one of Moscow’s leading oligarchs. Vienna had raised the case during negotiations over several previous sanctions packages. But people involved in the talks said this was the first time it had contributed to eleventh-hour delays. The Commission has sent Austria a proposal promising to examine the matter in a later sanctions package. Other governments succeeded in removing a proposed phaseout of Russian fish imports, despite anger that Moscow still earns more than half a billion dollars a year from sales to the EU. The initial proposal would have banned imports of cod, haddock and pollock. It was dropped after several countries raised concerns about consumer prices and the impact on the EU’s fish-processing industry. Earlier drafts also included sanctions against Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill and restrictions on former members of the Russian armed forces. Bulgaria opposed listing Kirill, the head of the Russian church and a prominent supporter of Moscow’s war. Italy also entered a formal reservation, with a fifth EU diplomat saying the Vatican opposed targeting the head of another church. Advertisement Advertisement “It’s Pope solidarity,” the diplomat said. Kirill was left out of the final text. France and Italy — both of which grant large numbers of visas to Russians — also objected to restrictions on former Russian soldiers. They argued that the system for establishing who should be covered was not ready to be implemented, and the measures were significantly watered down. While the carveouts have been significant, the package as it stands would result in dozens more Russian banks being cut off from the Western SWIFT messaging system. More than 250 people would also be banned from traveling to the EU in the largest such addition since 2023. “With freezing the oil price cap and the visa restrictions on soldiers, it is pretty ambitious,” the third diplomat said. Yet the concessions have punctured hopes that Orbán’s departure would make it substantially easier to tighten the economic pressure on Moscow. “Orbán was difficult,” said another EU diplomat, “but he never actually blocked whole packages.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/tunisia-s-activist.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said. Young Tunisians are increasingly unhappy with the government, while older Tunisians are more satisfied that a decade ago, according to one survey Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures . For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW. Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests . DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication. Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services. The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion." In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising . The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food. Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometer survey there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people. The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade. In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older. "What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39." Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%. "I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval." In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate. DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report. https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/08/t.text: TMT Newswire Media OutReach Newswire OTP Bank Becomes First EU Financial Institution to Open a EUR 7 Billion EMTN Programme on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange By Media OutReach Newswire October 8, 2026 10 Resize Small Medium Large Rated AAA on the China national scale by Lianhe and recently ranked 398th on Forbes Global 2000, up from 1007th in 2022 · Milestone marked by a gong ceremony at the Connect Hall, Hong Kong Stock Exchange, on 30 June 2026 BUDAPEST, HUNGARY and HONG KONG SAR - Media OutReach Newswire - 30 June 2026 - OTP Bank Plc. ("OTP Bank" or "OTP"), the leading banking group in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), today marked the establishment of its EUR 7 billion Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) programme on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited (the "Hong Kong Stock Exchange" or "HKEX") with a commemorative gong ceremony at the Connect Hall, Hong Kong Stock Exchange. OTP is the first European Union financial institution to open an EMTN programme on the exchange. Get the latest news delivered to your inbox Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy . Official OTP Bank Gong Ceremony The EUR 7 billion programme was established on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on 28 May 2026, following approval of its base prospectus by Luxembourg's Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) on 27 May 2026, allowing the issuer to raise debt in multiple tranches, currencies, structures and maturities over time. For OTP - which holds an AAA issuer rating on the China national scale from Lianhe Ratings, the highest available - it establishes a permanent platform for trading with certain OTP bonds, and later for raising capital from Asian institutional investors. Advertisement On 16 June 2026, OTP priced the programme's inaugural issuance: a EUR 1 billion Tier 2 note, listed in Hong Kong and Luxembourg. It is OTP's largest-ever bond transaction and, as at the issue date, the largest euro-denominated Tier 2 note issued by a bank in the CEE and wider CEMEA region. The offering drew a peak order book of EUR 4.1 billion - the largest in OTP's history - and priced at a coupon of 4.625%. The listing builds on OTP's growing presence in Asian capital markets. In 2025 OTP issued its first Dim Sum green bond, raising CNH 900 million and becoming the first Hungarian institution to issue a public offshore renminbi green bond, following a CNY 300 million bond in 2024. The Bank has operated a representative office in Beijing since 2017, became a full member of the Asian Financial Cooperation Association (AFCA) in 2024, and maintains a strategic partnership with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC). Advertisement Sándor Pataki, Director of Investor Relations and Capital Markets Operations of OTP Bank, said: "Listing our EMTN programme in Hong Kong is a clear demonstration of OTP Bank's long-term vision and strategic commitment to international capital markets. Hong Kong excels itself as one of the world's leading international financial centres, serving as a vital bridge between East and West. For OTP Bank, this is not only an opportunity to access liquidity, but also to deepen relationships and build lasting trust with investors in this dynamic region. The demand we have seen for OTP's credit, including the record order book for our inaugural issue off the programme, reflects the growing interest in high-quality European issuers." As Asian investors increasingly look to Europe to diversify their portfolios, Central and Eastern Europe offers a distinctive proposition: emerging-market growth rates combined with the low-risk profile of the European Union. The region's attractiveness is reinforced by its convergence towards the eurozone. Three of the five countries in which OTP is the market leader sit at the heart of Europe's euro-convergence story - Bulgaria, which adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, Slovenia, which adopted the euro years ago, and Hungary, OTP's flagship market, where the recently elected government aims to create the conditions for euro adoption around 2030. Advertisement OTP combines what rarely comes together in European banking: high growth, strong profitability and an ultraconservative balance sheet built for resilience. OTP Group is one of the largest and fastest-growing banking groups in the region, recently ranked 398th on the Forbes Global 2000 list, up from 1007th place in 2022. It pairs an annual organic loan growth of around 15% with a disciplined acquisition record and high profitability - a 2025 return on equity of 21.6% - and with an ultraconservative balance sheet: a leverage ratio well above its European peers, strong capital and liquidity, and one of the most resilient outcomes in the European Banking Authority's latest stress test. In 2023, OTP became the first European bank to enter Uzbekistan, bringing the total population across OTP's markets to 110 million. Sándor Pataki, Director of Investor Relations and Capital Markets Operations of OTP Bank, added: "We believe the combination of growth, profitability and stability is what makes OTP an attractive name for fixed-income investors. This is also reflected in our recent ranking among the world's top 500 companies by Forbes.These achievements are the result of a consistent strategy: prudent growth, diversified funding sources, and a strong focus on long-term partnerships. Over the decades, OTP Bank has built a solid track record in international debt capital markets, and today's milestones further strengthen that foundation. Looking ahead, we see significant opportunities to deepen our engagement with Asian investors and institutions. We are confident that this listing will serve as a cornerstone for long-term cooperation, mutual growth, and shared success." OTP has ranked No. 1 in Central and Eastern Europe by Tier 1 capital in The Banker's Top 100 CEE Banks for three consecutive years (2023-2025); it was named the second best-performing bank in Europe by S&P Global Market Intelligence and the Best Bank in Central and Eastern Europe by Global Finance. The Group has risen to 398th on the Forbes Global 2000 in 2026 (from 1007th in 2022). OTP Bank has been listed on the Budapest Stock Exchange since 1995. https://www.courant.com/2026/10/10/revie.text: Sebastian Stan in the movie “Fjord.” (Neon/Neon/TNS) By Tribune News Service | Tribune News Service PUBLISHED: October 10, 2026 at 11:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By Mark Olsen, Los Angeles Times Winner of the Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival, still among the most prestigious prizes any movie can claim, “Fjord” aims for both a quiet, subtle power and the directness of a sledgehammer. It speaks to the skill of Romanian writer-director Cristian Mungiu, along with the star power and acting prowess of its leads, Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, that the film achieves those goals, creating a mix of feelings including ambivalence, shock and dismay over what people will do to one another in the name of a common good. Having recently moved from Bucharest to a remote village in Norway, a conservative, devoutly Christian couple and their five young children have begun to insert themselves into the fabric of their new community. Mihai, the Romanian father (Stan), is a little intense and gloomy; Lisbet (Reinsve), a Norwegian, is shy but kind, and their focus seems clearly on what they see as a warm, loving homelife. But when their children are suddenly taken into protective custody over allegations of abuse, they find their world turned upside down. Eventually, the father asks a prosecutor with equal parts anger and exasperation, “Am I on trial for my beliefs?” The official answer to that question, more or less, is both no and yes. The government’s position is that the children cannot be placed back into a home where they will be harmed, whether that means physical violence or indoctrination in ideology counter to that of the state’s, such as no dancing, no internet and that being gay is wrong. Based on actual events involving a Romanian family in Norway in 2015, “Fjord” is purposefully designed to make a viewer — any viewer — question their assumptions and predispositions regarding the relationship between personal liberty and state power. While this may all sound a bit reactionary or like shooting fish in a barrel, Mungiu wisely complicates matters. The filmmaker, a previous Palme winner for his 2007 abortion drama “4 Weeks, 3 Months and 2 Days,” presumably knows that the majority of the audience for his international art-house domestic drama will be more aligned with the liberal, progressive politics of the Norwegian state than the religious, conservative couple at the story’s center. So most audiences will automatically be put into the purposefully uncomfortable position of siding with people they would never see themselves inclined to agree with. It is Mungiu’s sharpest and most illuminating maneuver. Once the story moves to the courtroom, “Fjord” begins to resemble 2023’s “Anatomy of a Fall” — another Cannes-winning champ released in the U.S. by boutique distributor Neon — for the way in which it allows American viewers a glimpse into another country’s legal system. It comes off as more conversational and slightly more chaotic than what we are used to in our own domestic courtroom procedurals. As the government prosecutor, Norwegian actor Christian Rubeck gives a smug and condescending tone to nearly every word out of his mouth, becoming the closest thing the movie has to a villain. Having previously appeared together in the offbeat comedy “A Different Man,” Stan and Reinsve keep the story from feeling like a dour exercise. As Mihai, Stan puts across a low-simmering rage at being put in the position of defending himself at all, while grappling with how to maintain what he sees as his natural role of patriarchal control. Reinsve, known for more outwardly dynamic roles in “The Worst Person in the World” and “Sentimental Value,” here conveys a subdued nuance as Lisbet struggles with understanding her place between her husband and her children. The moment when the couple’s infant child is taken from them by the authorities is devastating, each of them capturing a sense of helpless isolation from themselves, their community and each other. Special mention should also go to the performances by Vanessa Ceban and Jonathan Ciprian Breazu as the couple’s teenage children, also to Henrikke Lund-Olsen as a neighbor girl who becomes close to them. These young performers are the film’s secret weapon, since in practical, lived terms they bear the brunt of the existential hand-wringing on the part of all the adults. And too often they become an afterthought. The poster and key image from the film is a smiling snapshot of Mihai and Lisbet with their children, a seemingly happy family. Or are they? For a movie so steeped in ambiguity and nuance, it also often states its case quite plainly, such as when the couple’s lawyer says no one can really know what goes on in another family. The film asks one to look closer, not just at others but also at one’s own accepted opinions, assumptions and preconceptions. But it ends up with an outcome that feels as sadly inevitable as it is heartbreaking — an ethical knot that cannot be undone. ——— ‘FJORD’ (In English, Romanian, Norwegian and Swedish, with subtitles) No MPA rating Running time: 2:26 How to watch: Now in limited theatrical release ——— ©2026 Los Angeles Times. https://www.mfa.gov.lv/en/article/latvia.text: Latvian consular officials attend training on visa matters in Ankara Published: 14.10.2026. Flickr Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook X / Twitter Linkedin Threads On 14 and 15 October 2026, the annual training on visa matters for officials from Latvian diplomatic and consular missions abroad is taking place in Ankara, Türkiye. This year, consular officials from 21 Latvian missions that issue visas are participating in the training. Participants represent Latvian missions in Azerbaijan, Belarus, Canada, China, Egypt, France, Georgia, India, Ireland, Israel, Japan, Kazakhstan, Poland, Russia, Sweden, Turkey, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uzbekistan. The training aims to strengthen the knowledge and practical skills of consular officials at Latvian diplomatic missions in visa matters, with a particular focus on current migration and security challenges. During the training, participants develop their ability to identify illegal migration schemes and potential risks, familiarise themselves with risk profiles and learn about the latest trends in document forgery. Officials are also briefed on the latest amendments to migration legislation and improve their ability to assess visa applications in accordance with the principles of administrative procedure. “The effective assessment of visa applications is essential not only for ensuring high-quality consular services, but also for strengthening the security of Latvia and the European Union. It is therefore important that our consular officials regularly update their knowledge of current migration trends, document forgery methods and potential security risks,” emphasised Edīte Medne, Director of the Consular Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Experts from various Latvian institutions, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of Citizenship and Migration Affairs and the State Border Guard, as well as foreign experts, are delivering the training as lecturers. The annual training provides consular officials at Latvian diplomatic missions with an opportunity not only to enhance their professional knowledge, but also to share experiences and best practices with colleagues from other Latvian diplomatic missions, thereby promoting a consistent, high-quality assessment process for visa applications. The training is organised with financial support of the Instrument for Financial Support for Border Management and Visa Policy of the European Union within the framework of the project “Provision of regional training for consular officials of the Republic of Latvia on the EU uniform visa issuance policy in accordance with the requirements of the European Visa Code (Stage 1)” (Agreement No. ĀM/RPVP/2024/3). https://www.dw.com/en/megaspeed-and-the-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PI0v Prefer DW on Google The logo of data center company Megaspeed International at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026 Image: Taryn Ng/AFP Advertisement As Nvidia , one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy , attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for. Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba. According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system. This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China , because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes. Megaspeed's mega rise Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China. Megaspeed managed data centers for Chinese tech giant Alibaba Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China. At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing. On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026. "There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct." The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times , this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation. A brief history Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023. Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024. Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023. The relationship with Nvidia The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors. Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba. Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times. In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward. China and the battle for chips Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them. Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications. Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance. However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there. In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia's chips are seen as the gold standard for AI applications Image: Kobe Li/ZUMAPRESS/picture alliance In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips. In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment. However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.
